state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: What would happen if you tried your method on a simpler version of the problem with just two plants, one at \(10\) cm and the other at \(20\) cm?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, so if I have two plants, one at \(10\) cm and the other at \(20\) cm, the range is \(20 - 10 = 10\) cm. If I cut them both in half, they would be \(5\) cm and \(10\) cm, and the range would be \(10 - 5 = 5\) cm. So, I guess that means Tom was wrong. But what about Katie? If I add \(3\) cm to both, wouldn’t the range still be \(10\) cm? I'm a bit confused about that part.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: What would happen if you applied Katie's method to the simpler version of the problem with the two plants at \(10\) cm and \(20\) cm?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher effectively addresses the proportional change misconception by guiding the student to test both scenarios with simpler numbers, leading the student to self-correct about multiplication (Tom) and recognize that addition preserves range (Katie), though the final turn ends before complete resolution.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher perfectly exemplifies the Socratic method by using only probing questions to guide the student toward discovering their own errors, never providing direct answers, and effectively using a simpler counterexample to expose the flaw in the student's reasoning about Tom's claim.
